title: “YOUR MONEY PERISH WITH YOU”—THE TERRIFYING MOMENT A MAN TRIED TO PUT A PRICE ON THE POWER OF GOD
paragraphs: “YOUR MONEY PERISH WITH YOU”—THE TERRIFYING MOMENT A MAN TRIED TO PUT A PRICE ON THE POWER OF GOD

Simon saw something extraordinary in Samaria. He had money in his hands, apostles standing before him, and the power of God unfolding before his eyes. Then Peter spoke words severe enough to expose a temptation that still walks through churches, ministries, platforms, and human hearts today: What happens when we begin wanting what comes from God more than we want God Himself?
There are sentences in Scripture that comfort you.
There are sentences that carry you when grief has emptied the room and you no longer know how to pray.
And then there are sentences that stop you cold.
This is one of them.
“Your money perish with you.”
Imagine hearing those words from the apostle Peter.
Not from an enemy.
Not from someone mocking your faith.
From a man who had walked with Jesus.
A man who had watched Christ touch lepers, forgive sinners, confront religious hypocrisy, carry a cross, die under Roman execution, and rise again.
And Peter was not talking to a pagan who had never heard the Gospel.
He was talking to Simon.
A man who had believed Philip’s preaching and had been baptized.
That should make every Christian read more slowly.
Because Acts 8 is not merely a story about one strange man in ancient Samaria who made one terrible offer.
It holds up a mirror.
And if we are courageous enough to stand in front of it, we may discover that Simon’s temptation did not die with Simon.
It simply learned how to dress differently.
The story begins with a man accustomed to attention.

Acts 8 describes Simon as someone who had previously practiced magic in Samaria and astonished the people. He presented himself as someone great, and people paid attention to him. They were so impressed that they associated him with extraordinary power.
Then Philip arrived.
And suddenly Simon encountered something he could not manufacture.
Philip did not come preaching Philip.
He preached Christ.
Acts 8:5 says Philip went down to the city of Samaria and proclaimed Christ to them.
That changes everything.
The center of genuine Christian ministry is never the charisma of the messenger.
Never the size of the platform.
Never the personality.
Never the brand.
Never the merchandise.
Never the bank account.
Never the applause.
Jesus Christ is the center.

Philip preached the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ. Men and women believed and were baptized. Simon himself believed, was baptized, and continued with Philip, astonished by the signs and great miracles taking place.
Think about that.
The man who had once astonished everyone was now astonished himself.
The performer had found a power he could not perform.
The man accustomed to impressing others was now watching works that left him speechless.
Then Peter and John came from Jerusalem.
They prayed for the Samaritan believers, laid hands on them, and the Holy Spirit was given.
Simon saw what happened.
And something inside him moved.
But what moved inside him was precisely the problem.
Scripture says:
“Ἰδὼν δὲ ὁ Σίμων ὅτι διὰ τῆς ἐπιθέσεως τῶν χειρῶν τῶν ἀποστόλων δίδοται τὸ πνεῦμα, προσήνεγκεν αὐτοῖς χρήματα.”
In context, Acts 8:18 means:
“When Simon saw that the Spirit was given through the laying on of the apostles’ hands, he offered them money.”
Money.
Simon looked at the work of the Holy Spirit…
and reached for his wallet.
He said, in essence, “Give me this authority too.”
Do not rush past that.
Simon was not merely asking for prayer.
He wanted the ability associated with what he had witnessed.
He saw spiritual power and apparently imagined that money could obtain it.
Perhaps the old Simon was still breathing underneath the newly baptized Simon.
The old hunger to be somebody.
The old fascination with power.
The old attraction to influence.
The old desire to possess what made crowds look in his direction.
And suddenly Peter answered.
The Greek of Acts 8:20 is devastating:
“Τὸ ἀργύριόν σου σὺν σοὶ εἴη εἰς ἀπώλειαν, ὅτι τὴν δωρεὰν τοῦ θεοῦ ἐνόμισας διὰ χρημάτων κτᾶσθαι.”
A direct rendering is:
“May your silver be with you unto destruction, because you thought the gift of God could be acquired through money.”
The familiar English force of it is unforgettable:
“Your money perish with you.”
But Peter was not declaring that money itself is inherently evil.
Scripture does not teach that.
The problem was Simon’s heart and what he believed money could do.
Peter tells him why.
“You thought the gift of God could be acquired through money.”
There it is.
The scandal.
Simon had encountered grace…
and instinctively tried to turn it into a transaction.
And perhaps that is where this ancient story suddenly becomes painfully modern.
Because human beings still try to negotiate with God.
We just use different currency.
“God, if I give enough, will You finally love me?”
“If I serve enough, will You overlook what I did?”
“If I attend church enough, will You owe me a blessing?”
“If I become successful enough, will that prove You approve of me?”
“If I donate enough, will You make my prayer happen?”
“If I look spiritual enough, can I avoid confronting what is actually inside me?”
“If people admire my ministry, does that mean my heart must be right?”
And sometimes the currency is not money at all.
Sometimes we pay with performance.
Reputation.
Religious activity.
Followers.
Titles.
Connections.
Public generosity.
Bible knowledge.
Even ministry.
We place our achievements on the counter and quietly ask heaven:
“Is this enough to buy what I need?”
And the cross answers:
You cannot buy it.
Because Jesus already paid.
That is the difference between the Gospel and every human attempt to save ourselves.
The Gospel does not announce that spiritually impressive people can purchase their way upward.
The Gospel announces that God came down.
We were sinners unable to purchase reconciliation with God, so Christ did what our morality, reputation, religious activity, and money could never accomplish.
He gave Himself.
Peter knew this better than most.
Years earlier, Peter himself had failed spectacularly.
He had promised loyalty to Jesus.
Then came the courtyard.
Questions.
Fear.
Denial.
“I do not know the man.”
Again.
Again.
Again.
Then the rooster.
Imagine Peter’s shame.
Imagine remembering the face of the Christ you swore you would never abandon.
Peter could not purchase his way out of that courtyard.
He could not donate enough to erase three denials.
He could not perform enough miracles to rewrite what he had done.
Peter needed grace.
And after the resurrection, Jesus came for him.
That is why Peter’s warning to Simon must never be separated from the Gospel Peter himself had received.
Peter was not a flawless man looking down upon a dirty sinner.
He was a restored sinner confronting another man whose heart desperately needed God.
Peter continued:
“You have neither part nor lot in this matter, for your heart is not right before God.”
Then came the command Simon desperately needed.
“Repent.”
Not:
Pay more.
Not:
Build your reputation.
Not:
Prove yourself.
Not:
Purchase another opportunity.
Repent.
Acts 8:22 records Peter telling Simon to repent of his wickedness and pray to the Lord that, if possible, the intention of his heart might be forgiven.
That is a hard word.
But it is also mercy.
Because exposure is not always rejection.
Sometimes exposure is the mercy that interrupts us before our hidden desires destroy us.
There are moments when God loves us too deeply to let us remain comfortable with the thing killing our souls.
The Holy Spirit may put His finger on the secret ambition.
The hidden greed.
The obsession with recognition.
The addiction nobody knows about.
The bitterness we have baptized as “discernment.”
The pride disguised as standards.
The envy disguised as concern.
The hunger for spiritual power without the willingness to surrender.
And it hurts.
Of course it hurts.
Surgery hurts too.
But the Surgeon cuts because something precious is worth saving.
Peter tells Simon, “I see that you are in the gall of bitterness and in the bond of iniquity.”
Bondage.
That is what sin eventually does.
It promises control and becomes your master.
It promises pleasure and demands another payment.
It promises significance and makes you terrified of becoming insignificant.
It promises freedom and slowly builds a prison around the heart.
Maybe your prison does not look like Simon’s.
Maybe nobody suspects yours exists.
You still smile.
Still post the verse.
Still say, “God is good.”
Still show up.
Still know when to lift your hands.
Still know Christian vocabulary.
But privately?
You are exhausted.
There is something between you and God, and you know its name.
Perhaps money has become your security.
Perhaps success has become your identity.
Perhaps ministry has become the place where you secretly need applause.
Perhaps you are following Jesus partly because you hope He will give you the life you actually worship.
Perhaps you want His gifts more than His presence.
Perhaps you want His power without His holiness.
His promises without His lordship.
His heaven without His cross.
His forgiveness without repentance.
And perhaps the frightening part is that you can live around Christian things long enough to stop noticing the difference.
Simon had been baptized.
Simon stayed near Philip.
Simon watched miracles.
Simon witnessed apostolic ministry.
Yet Peter still went directly to the condition of his heart.
That should humble us.
Proximity to holy things is not the same as surrender to a holy God.
A Bible in your hand cannot substitute for Christ ruling your heart.
A church seat cannot repent for you.
A Christian family cannot believe for you.
A ministry position cannot sanctify secret sin.
A donation cannot purchase forgiveness.
And no Christian ministry worthy of the Gospel should ever tell you otherwise.
You cannot buy the Holy Spirit.
You cannot buy salvation.
You cannot purchase an answered prayer.
You cannot buy a miracle.
You cannot pay your way into heaven.
You cannot make God owe you because you financially supported His work.
Grace ceases to be grace the moment we imagine it can be purchased.
Jesus Christ is not for sale.
And neither is His blood.
The apostle Peter later wrote that believers were redeemed not with corruptible things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ.
There is the answer to Simon’s silver.
Silver could not redeem Simon.
Gold cannot redeem you.
Christ can.
The currency at Calvary was not your money.
It was His blood.
The price was not paid by the sinner climbing toward God.
It was paid by the Son of God giving Himself for sinners.
This is why the Gospel can reach the person who thinks he has ruined everything.
Maybe that person is you.
Maybe there are chapters in your life you would burn if memories could be destroyed.
Maybe you have manipulated people.
Maybe greed got into your heart.
Maybe pornography hollowed out your secret life.
Maybe adultery shattered what you promised to protect.
Maybe pride made you cruel.
Maybe religion made you self-righteous.
Maybe money became the god you would never call a god.
Maybe you have spent years presenting a version of yourself that does not exist when the door closes.
And somewhere beneath all the pretending is one terrifying question:
“If Jesus knew everything, would He still want me?”
He already knows.
That is what makes grace so scandalous.
Christ did not go to the cross because humanity was secretly better than it appeared.
He went because our condition was worse than we wanted to admit—and His mercy was greater than we dared imagine.
The cross tells the truth about both.
Your sin was serious enough that Christ had to die.
His love was great enough that He willingly did.
And the resurrection announces that sin, shame, death, and the grave do not get the final sentence over everyone who comes to Christ.
Jesus does.
This is where scandal becomes grace.
Peter knew the scandal of denial.
Christ wrote restoration.
Paul knew the scandal of persecuting believers.
Christ wrote apostleship and mission.
The thief beside Jesus knew the scandal of a condemned life.
Christ spoke hope to a dying man who could no longer build a respectable religious résumé.
Again and again, Scripture refuses to pretend sin is harmless.
But Scripture also refuses to pretend sin is stronger than the Savior.
That is why repentance is not God saying, “Clean yourself up so perhaps I will tolerate you.”
Repentance is the sinner turning from sin toward the God whose mercy is found in Jesus Christ.
You stop defending what Christ died to save you from.
You stop calling darkness light.
You stop negotiating.
You stop hiding.
You come empty-handed.
No spiritual résumé.
No bargaining chips.
No silver.
Just:
“Jesus, have mercy on me.”
And He is not a reluctant Savior.
First John 1:9 teaches that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive us and cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
Jesus said in John 6:37 that the one who comes to Him He will never cast out.
Read that again if shame has been telling you to stay away.
Come.
Not because your sin is small.
Come because Christ is sufficient.
Come because the blood shed at Calvary is greater than the stain you cannot remove yourself.
Come because the tomb is empty.
Come because Jesus still saves sinners.
Come because grace is not permission to remain chained.
Grace breaks chains.
Maybe Simon’s story disturbed you because you recognized something.
Sit with it.
Ask the question most of us avoid:
“What do I actually want from Jesus?”
Do I want Him…
or merely what I believe He can give me?
If God removed the applause, would I still worship?
If the promotion never came, would He still be worthy?
If the healing took longer than I hoped, would Christ still be Lord?
If nobody knew my name, would knowing His be enough?
If following Jesus cost me instead of advancing me, would I follow?
Those questions expose things.
Mine too.
Because Simon’s story is not ammunition for pointing at prosperity preachers, corrupt ministries, wealthy Christians, poor Christians, famous pastors, or somebody else we already dislike.
The safest way to read Acts 8 is not:
“Thank God I am not Simon.”
It is:
“Lord, search me.”
Search my motives.
Search my giving.
Search my ministry.
Search my ambition.
Search what I secretly want people to think about me.
Search what I believe money can secure.
Search what I want from You.
And where You find Simon hiding in me…
bring me to repentance.
That prayer is dangerous.
It is also freeing.
Because the Christian life was never supposed to be an exhausting project of protecting an image.
At the foot of the cross, there is finally nowhere left to perform.
You are known.
You are exposed.
You are invited to repent.
And in Christ, there is grace.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to tell strangers every private detail. But you also do not have to pretend conviction never happened.
Someone reading silently may need to discover that repentance is not the end of the story.
It can be where restoration begins.
Not because sharing a Gospel Warrior article earns favor with God.
It does not.
Not because an algorithm can measure your devotion.
It cannot.
Share because somebody you love may be quietly becoming Simon.
Someone may be trying to purchase with performance what can only be received through Christ.
Someone may be surrounded by Christianity while privately drifting from Jesus.
Someone may need to hear tonight that repentance is still possible.
There may come a night when ambition starts whispering again.
A night when money begins feeling more trustworthy than God.
A night when shame tells you to hide.
Come back and remember Simon.
Come back and remember Peter.
Come back and remember the cross.

We want this community to be a place where people encounter daily Scripture, conviction, encouragement, biblical truth, healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment centered not on personalities, but on Jesus Christ.
It does not purchase God’s favor.
It does not purchase the Holy Spirit.
It does not make God owe you a blessing.
Jesus purchased redemption. We never could.

Sharing this article publicly is another. Prayer is another. Telling someone about Jesus is another. Faithful generosity should flow from love for God, not pressure, fear, or an attempt to purchase spiritual reward.
But never confuse supporting the messenger with purchasing the Message.
The Gospel was bought at a price you could never afford…
and then offered to repentant sinners as grace.
Simon reached for silver.
Peter pointed toward repentance.
And Jesus still stands at the center of the story.
So perhaps the most important question is no longer what Simon wanted to buy.
Perhaps it is what you have been trying to buy from God.
Approval?
Security?
Influence?
Forgiveness?
A clean conscience?
A second chance?
Put the silver down.
Put the performance down.
Put the religious résumé down.
Put the secret bargaining down.
You cannot purchase resurrection.
You cannot purchase grace.
You cannot purchase the love of God.
Come to Jesus.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Receive what money could never buy.
And then, because you have received grace, live generously—not to purchase God, but because in Christ you have discovered a treasure money could never contain.
“Jesus, search my heart.”
Sometimes the most dangerous thing in your hand is not the money you are holding—it is the secret belief that there is something Jesus will give you only after you prove you deserve Him.
But at Calvary, empty hands were always the only hands capable of receiving grace.
